sources.note: Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-17. Quoted: 'Neither the key policy nor the IAM policy alone is sufficient - you must change both'; the key policy in the owning account must give the external account (or its roles) permission; IAM policies in the external account delegate it, and can only grant actions the key policy also allows. The KMS guide (read 2026-11-18): 'AWS KMS retains all key material for a KMS key ... AWS KMS deletes key material only when you delete the KMS key', and decryption automatically uses the version that encrypted the data (rotate-keys.html); 'You cannot change the key policies of AWS managed keys' (key-policy-modifying.html).

brief.situation: You are the solutions architect at Northgate Clinical Research, a fictional trial sponsor. The data account (111122223333) shares trial results with the analytics account (444455556666) through the bucket s3://ngcr-trial-share, encrypted with the customer managed key share-key, as the sponsor's data protection plan requires. The analytics role can list the bucket but every read fails. The safety report to the regulator is built from this data at 09:00.
handover: Last week the data team switched the bucket's default encryption from SSE-S3 to share-key; new objects since then use the key.
The data protection plan requires customer managed keys with automatic rotation for trial data.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the diagram shows the share bucket, its KMS key and the analytics role in the other account.
Each command takes a minute or two; the clock moves only when you act or wait.
When you close, you write the record and explain your reasoning.

effects.log: Cross-account use of a KMS key needs both: the key policy in the owning account allows the role, and the role's own policy delegates Decrypt on that one key. Only Decrypt and DescribeKey: the analytics account reads, it does not encrypt.

writeup.question: For the record: why the reads failed after the switch to share-key, what you granted, and how the plan's requirements are met.

parts.label: Why
parts.criteria: Places the denial at KMS, not S3.
parts.modelAnswer: Since last week new objects use share-key. Reading them makes S3 call kms:Decrypt for the analytics role; CloudTrail showed KMS refusing because the key policy names only the data account, and the role had no kms:Decrypt either.

parts.label: Grant
parts.modelAnswer: Added analytics-reader to the key policy with Decrypt and DescribeKey, and kms:Decrypt on that key ARN to the role's policy. Copying the data to SSE-S3 would have taken it out of the key's controls.

parts.label: Plan
parts.criteria: Meets rotation and records the change.
parts.modelAnswer: Automatic rotation is now on (old objects still decrypt), and the grant is recorded for the data protection plan.

unprotected.headline: The deadline met by breaking the plan
unprotected.body: The key is the control the plan relies on: access decided in its policy, every Decrypt logged, revocable in one place. Grant the reader on the key instead of moving the data out from under it.

filingLate.headline: Two policies, both needed
filingLate.body: For a key in another account, the key policy must allow the external role and the role's IAM policy must allow Decrypt on that key. S3 permissions alone do not reach KMS.

granted.headline: Good: both sides of a cross-account key
granted.body: You read the KMS denial, found the key policy and the role both missing Decrypt, granted the minimum on both sides, checked the read, and turned on the rotation the plan requires.

gaps.body: The criteria show what was left: the evidence before the change, the lasting step, the check, or the cause in the record.

scoring.modelReasoning: Old SSE-S3 objects read and new share-key objects fail, and CloudTrail shows KMS refusing Decrypt, so the problem is the key, not the bucket. A key in another account needs both the key policy to allow the external role and that role's IAM policy to allow Decrypt on the key; grant only Decrypt and DescribeKey. Copying data to SSE-S3 escapes the plan's controls; more S3 permissions do nothing. Then turn on the rotation the plan requires and record the grant.
